strengths: Assuming the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the paper offers an original and potentially useful formulation: reinforcement-learning a multi-image editor with feedback from a frozen 3D foundation model, avoiding scarce paired 3D-editing supervision and per-scene optimization.

The reward design is intuitively motivated and combines complementary signals: VGGT depth/point confidence for geometric coherence, relative-pose preservation, and an anchor-view LPIPS reward intended to prevent the trivial blurry-output solution.

The method is clearly presented, and the reported results are promising: RL3DEdit improves VIEScore from 3.23 to 5.48 over the FLUX-Kontext version of EditSplat, slightly improves the reported reprojection loss, and reduces editing time from 40 to 1.5 minutes on the stated hardware.

Ablations address the main reward components and compare VGGT feedback with SfM- and reprojection-based alternatives. The examples convincingly illustrate how purely geometric objectives can be reward-hacked through texture removal or smoothing.
The inclusion of geometry-changing edits, unseen instructions/scenes, and a preliminary Qwen-Image-Edit result suggests broader applicability than methods constrained by source depth maps.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is too limited for the broad claims. Training uses only eight scenes, while the evaluation contains just 100 cases and partly reuses the training scenes and instructions. Cases derived from multiple views of the same few scenes are highly correlated, yet no scene-level aggregation, variance, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are reported.

The principal consistency metric is not sufficiently independent of the training signal: Ph-Loss uses VGGT-predicted depth, while VGGT also supplies the optimization rewards. This risks circular evaluation. Ground-truth-geometry error, correspondence-based metrics from an independent model, or controlled synthetic scenes are needed.

Figure 5 does not establish that VGGT confidence reliably measures the target notion of consistency. It progressively mixes original views with independently edited views, confounding geometric inconsistency with appearance/domain changes and the number of outliers. The study reports only averaged confidence and no correlation against independently measured geometric error across edit types, scene types, or natural failure modes.

Evidence for actual 3D and multi-view quality is weak in the supplied manuscript. Most qualitative comparisons show one or two small views, while the claimed user study, per-split results, reconstruction details, verifier definitions, and other essential protocol information are deferred to an appendix that is not included. This prevents assessment of view interpolation, temporal camera trajectories, floaters, and reconstruction artifacts.

The comparison is incomplete and potentially confounded. Most baselines use the much weaker InstructPix2Pix backbone; only EditSplat is reimplemented with FLUX-Kontext, and its unusually large 40-minute runtime is not explained in enough detail. The recent Tinker method discussed as a strong FLUX-based competitor is omitted. It is also unclear whether all timing entries include the same rendering and 3DGS-reconstruction stages.

VIEScore is described as reproducible and objective merely because it uses GPT-4.1, which is not justified. No exact evaluator prompt, model snapshot, repeated-query variance, blinded human validation, or failure analysis is supplied. CLIP-directional similarity and VIEScore alone provide limited support for instruction fidelity and identity preservation.

The Qwen-Image-Edit experiment is underspecified and evaluated only in the restricted face-only ablation setting. It therefore does not substantiate the claim that the framework transfers seamlessly to other backbones.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate: important GRPO details, reward normalization and constants such as lambda, prompt filtering, sampling strategy, 3DGS reconstruction settings, test splits, and baseline reimplementation details are absent from the supplied paper. A promise to release code does not resolve these omissions.

The bibliography contains serious attribution errors. Most notably, citation [48], repeatedly presented as the VGGT foundation model, is actually titled “Statistical characteristics of the proton isotropy boundary,” while [15] is cited for streaming/causal 3D perception but duplicates a monocular-depth reference. Several other entries are duplicated with altered arXiv identifiers. These errors undermine scholarly attribution and make key components difficult to verify.

The limitations section acknowledges context length and compute but omits more consequential concerns: reliance on VGGT's domain biases, possible reward hacking not covered by the tested alternatives, circular evaluation, dependence on accurate input cameras, stochastic anchor bias, and failure under large topology or visibility changes. Overall, the core idea is promising, but stronger independent evaluation and corrected, reproducible documentation are required before the scientific case is convincing.

strengths: The core framing is interesting and relevant: using reinforcement learning because multi-view consistency may be easier to verify than to supervise with paired 3D-edit data is a plausible research direction.

The proposed reward combines depth/point confidence, relative camera pose, and a single-view quality anchor. The component ablations provide some evidence that these terms address different failure modes.

The method targets a useful combination of semantic flexibility and efficiency, and the manuscript reports results across several edit types, an additional Qwen-based editor, and both seen and unseen conditions.
The paper is generally readable, provides several implementation details, and acknowledges limitations involving context length and training cost.
weaknesses: The central technical premise is not validated rigorously. Figure 5 merely replaces consistent source views with independently edited images; declining VGGT confidence may reflect appearance distribution shifts, semantic disagreement, texture, or occlusion rather than geometric inconsistency. There is no evaluation against controlled geometric corruptions, human consistency judgments, or ground-truth geometry, nor evidence that VGGT remains reliable after direct reward optimization.

The evaluation split provides weak evidence of generalization. Seventy of 100 cases reuse training scenes and instructions and differ only in viewpoint; only 16 cases use unseen instructions and 14 use new scenes. Results are aggregated across these substantially different regimes, with no uncertainty, repeated runs, or statistical testing.

The improvement attributable specifically to RL is unclear. Most baselines use the much weaker InstructPix2Pix backbone, while the only FLUX baseline is a reimplementation of EditSplat. A direct, untrained FLUX-Kontext multi-image baseline is essential because FLUX already provides the cross-view interaction credited with enabling consistency. The closely related Tinker method is discussed but not evaluated.

The metrics are insufficient for the claims. Calling GPT-4.1-based VIEScore reproducible and objective is unjustified without the exact evaluator prompt, settings, repetitions, and version. CLIP directional similarity weakly measures edit correctness, while the definition and depth source for Ph-Loss are absent and may favor a method trained with VGGT-derived geometry. A user study is claimed to exist in an appendix, but no appendix is included.

Qualitative evidence is too limited to establish multi-view or reconstructed-3D consistency: most examples show only one or two small rendered views. There are no trajectories, cross-view correspondences, geometry visualizations, or reconstruction-quality measurements. The face-only ablations use roughly 200 samples and provide neither multiple seeds nor variance.

Reproducibility is poor. Numerous essential details are deferred to a nonexistent appendix, including the formal GRPO objective, reward and optimizer hyperparameters, quality-filtering procedure, dataset splits, baseline adaptation, SfM/Ph-Loss definitions, and 3DGS reconstruction settings. Code and models are only promised for future release.

The bibliography contains consequential attribution errors: the cited VGGT reference is an unrelated proton-isotropy paper; the citation used for streaming/causal 3D attention duplicates a monocular-depth paper; Qwen-Image-Edit is cited as ReasonEdit; and several works have duplicate entries. This prevents reliable verification of the method and related-work claims.

The claims of a robust verifier, state-of-the-art performance, strong zero-shot generalization, and an optimization-free single-pass 3D editor exceed the evidence. In particular, the final 3D reconstruction stage is largely unspecified and may itself involve optimization. The promising idea therefore does not yet form a convincing, reproducible scientific case for acceptance.

strengths: The paper presents an original and well-motivated Algorithms/General contribution: using reinforcement learning with a frozen 3D foundation model as a verifier offers a plausible way to learn multi-view consistency without scarce paired 3D-editing supervision.

The reward design is thoughtful. Depth/point confidence, relative-pose preservation, and a single-view quality anchor address complementary failure modes, while the comparison against SfM and reprojection rewards usefully demonstrates reward hacking.

The reported results are strong: RL3DEdit improves VIEScore from 3.23 to 5.48 over the FLUX-Kontext EditSplat baseline, achieves the best CLIP-direction and photometric consistency scores, and reduces editing time from 40 to 1.5 minutes under the stated setup.

Qualitative examples cover meaningful geometry-changing operations—including object addition, motion, replacement, and scene restyling—and generally show cleaner, more faithful edits than the baselines. The component ablations are directionally consistent with the method's rationale.
The method requires no per-scene or per-prompt fine-tuning at inference, and the preliminary Qwen-Image-Edit result suggests that the framework may transfer across editing backbones.
weaknesses: The empirical scale is limited and insufficiently characterized: training uses only eight scenes, while the 100 evaluation 'cases' are not broken down into independent scenes, prompts, and views in the supplied manuscript. Seventy cases appear closely related to the training protocol, and only 14 evaluate new scenes, making the broad generalization and state-of-the-art claims less secure.

Evaluation relies heavily on a proprietary GPT-4.1-based VIEScore without reporting prompts, repeated judgments, uncertainty, or statistical significance. CLIP-direction is also weak for spatial and geometric correctness, while photometric reprojection can favor blur. A larger blinded user study and stronger geometry-aware metrics should appear in the main evidence.

Several important details are deferred to an appendix that is absent from the supplied PDF, including the exact GRPO objective, reconstruction procedure, data splits, prompt list, baseline reimplementation, metric definition, per-split results, and user study. This substantially limits reproducibility and prevents close scrutiny of the comparison.

The ablations are trained only on face scenes with roughly 200 samples, so they do not establish that the reward components behave similarly for the diverse scene-level and geometry-changing edits central to the paper. Results also lack multiple seeds or training-variance analysis despite potentially unstable RL optimization.

The verifier analysis degrades consistency by progressively mixing independently edited and original views, which is a relatively artificial corruption. It does not test whether VGGT confidence reliably ranks subtler real failure modes, nor whether optimization exploits biases in VGGT on unseen domains.

The bibliography contains serious attribution errors: reference 48, cited throughout as VGGT, is instead a proton-isotropy paper; reference 15 does not support the claimed streaming/causal-attention statement; and multiple entries are duplicated with inconsistent identifiers. These are correctable but presently undermine scholarly reliability.

The paper omits comparisons with some closely related recent methods discussed in its own related-work section, notably Tinker, and therefore should qualify its state-of-the-art claim. Overall, the core idea and preliminary evidence favor acceptance, but the limited evaluation and missing reproducibility details keep the recommendation borderline.

strengths: The paper presents an original and compelling Algorithms/General contribution: using a frozen 3D foundation model as a verifier for reinforcement-learning-based multi-view editing is a well-motivated way to bypass scarce paired 3D editing data.

The method is technically coherent. VGGT depth/point confidence, relative-pose preservation, and an anchor-view fidelity reward address complementary failure modes, and the ablations show substantial degradation when these components are removed.

The empirical results are strong: RL3DEdit substantially improves VIEScore (5.48 versus 3.23 for the strongest FLUX-based baseline), CLIP directional similarity, and user preference, while achieving competitive multi-view consistency and much lower runtime. Qualitative results cover additions, replacements, motion, style, and background edits.

The evaluation includes 100 cases, unseen instructions, unseen scenes, a 25-participant user study, backbone transfer to Qwen-Image-Edit, alternative verifier comparisons, and several design ablations. The zero-shot results are particularly encouraging given only eight training scenes and 1,319 samples.

The manuscript is clear and visually effective, provides useful implementation and dataset details in the supplement, and candidly discusses limitations involving context length, large non-rigid deformation, and training cost.
weaknesses: The consistency evaluation is not sufficiently independent of the training signal. The principal Ph-Loss uses VGGT-predicted depths, while VGGT confidence is also central to the reward. Moreover, the reported advantage is very small (0.076 versus 0.077 for GaussCtrl). Evaluation using independently estimated or ground-truth geometry, correspondence metrics, or reconstruction accuracy would make the consistency claim substantially more convincing.

The evidence that VGGT confidence specifically measures multi-view consistency is limited. The controlled study progressively substitutes independently edited images, simultaneously changing consistency, appearance distribution, and edit severity. It lacks comparisons between equally realistic consistent and inconsistent edited sets, uncertainty estimates, or quantitative correlation against an independent consistency ground truth.

The main in-distribution split uses the same eight scenes and 70 prompts as training, changing only viewpoints. Although the 30 zero-shot cases are helpful, they comprise just four new scenes and 14 scene-level examples. Broader evaluation is needed to establish the claimed general 3D consistency prior, especially for stylized edits and severe geometry changes; stylized performance is discussed without quantitative results.

The comparison omits the highly relevant Tinker method despite discussing it extensively and making state-of-the-art claims. The custom EditSplat-plus-FLUX baseline is useful, but its implementation fidelity is not independently validated. Broader comparisons to recent feed-forward multi-view editors would improve fairness.

The paper repeatedly describes the method as “single-pass” and “optimization-free,” yet producing the final editable 3D representation uses AnySplat initialization followed by 3,000 iterations of per-scene 3DGS optimization. The editor itself avoids per-scene fine-tuning, but the current wording overstates the end-to-end property.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: important optimization parameters such as learning rate, KL coefficient, clipping threshold, batch scheduling, and random-seed variability are not reported. Ablations are trained only on one face scene with roughly 200 samples, with no repeated runs or error bars, so their generality and statistical reliability are uncertain.

The user-study protocol lacks demographic information, randomization/blinding details, per-participant trial counts, agreement statistics, and confidence intervals. VIEScore also depends on GPT-4.1, so it is not fully reproducible without model-version and prompting details.

strengths: The central idea is original and well motivated: using a frozen 3D foundation model as a verifier allows reinforcement learning to improve multi-view editing without requiring paired 3D editing targets.

The method combines complementary signals—VGGT depth/point confidence, relative-pose agreement, and a single-view anchor—and the component ablations show substantial degradation when these signals are removed.

The paper addresses a relevant computer-vision problem and demonstrates varied edit types, including additions, appearance changes, and some geometry-changing edits. Updating EditSplat with FLUX-Kontext is also a useful attempt to separate gains from those of the stronger 2D backbone.

The presentation is generally clear, the reconstruction procedure and training set are documented in the supplement, and the authors include comparisons against alternative consistency rewards, failure cases, and practical runtime measurements.
weaknesses: The central premise that VGGT confidence reliably measures multi-view consistency is not convincingly validated. Figure 5 replaces views with independently generated images involving different semantic changes, simultaneously altering consistency, content, realism, and distribution shift. The reported confidence decline therefore does not isolate 3D inconsistency. There is no evaluation against ground-truth geometric errors, controlled perturbations, or human consistency judgments.

The evaluation has substantial train/test overlap. Seventy of the 100 cases use both scenes and editing instructions seen during training and change only the rendered viewpoint. Another 16 use new instructions on the same eight training scenes, leaving only 14 cases across four genuinely unseen scenes. This is too narrow to support the paper's broad claims of arbitrary-instruction and scene-level generalization.

The consistency evaluation is partly circular. The method is trained using VGGT-derived signals, while Ph-Loss—the principal quantitative consistency metric—also uses depths inferred by VGGT. Moreover, the paper acknowledges that this metric can reward blurred images, yet provides no independent geometric metric or sufficiently rigorous perceptual evaluation to resolve the concern.

VIEScore relies on the closed GPT-4.1 model, but the evaluation prompt, sampling settings, number of runs, output parsing, and score variability are not reported. Calling this assessment objective and reproducible is therefore not justified. CLIP directional similarity also depends on source-scene text descriptions whose construction is not adequately specified.

The user study is underreported: although 25 participants are mentioned, the number of judgments per case, participant allocation, randomization, tie handling, quality control, and statistical uncertainty are absent. The large preference advantage consequently cannot be assessed for significance or possible presentation bias.

The baseline comparison does not cleanly establish method-level superiority. Most baselines retain the much weaker InstructPix2Pix backbone, while only EditSplat receives the FLUX-Kontext upgrade. The custom FLUX implementation is described only briefly, with no evidence of comparable tuning. The paper also omits stronger controlled baselines such as multi-image FLUX-Kontext followed by the identical AnySplat/3DGS reconstruction without RL.

The claims of a 'single-pass' and 'optimization-free' 3D editing system are misleading. Although multi-view image editing uses one model invocation, the final scene still requires AnySplat initialization followed by 3,000 iterations of per-scene 3DGS optimization. The method also assumes nine overlapping views and known ground-truth camera poses, limitations that materially narrow its applicability.

Results lack uncertainty estimates or repeated training runs, despite expensive and potentially unstable RL optimization. Most ablations are restricted to one face scene and roughly 200 samples, and the asserted transfer to Qwen-Image-Edit lacks sufficient training and implementation detail. Together with the small custom test set, this leaves the reported large gains insufficiently substantiated for an Algorithms/General contribution.

strengths: The paper presents a timely and original Algorithms/General contribution: using reinforcement learning with a frozen 3D foundation model as a verifier offers a compelling way to learn multi-view-consistent editing without paired 3D editing supervision.

The central “edit in 2D, verify in 3D” insight is intuitive and potentially impactful. The combination of VGGT depth/point confidence, relative-pose consistency, and an anchor reward is technically well motivated.

The empirical results are strong. RL3DEdit substantially improves VIEScore (5.48 versus 3.23 for the strongest FLUX-based baseline), CLIP directional similarity, photometric consistency, and editing time. Qualitative comparisons also show visibly better instruction following and fewer ghosting artifacts.

The experiments address diverse edit types, including additions, replacements, motion, materials, styles, and background changes. Tests on unseen instructions and four unseen scenes provide encouraging evidence of generalization beyond the training combinations.

The ablations support the principal design choices: removing geometric, pose, or anchor rewards degrades performance, while SfM and photometric rewards exhibit plausible reward-hacking behavior. Results with Qwen-Image-Edit suggest that the framework is not entirely tied to FLUX-Kontext.

The paper is clearly organized, candidly discusses limitations such as severe non-rigid deformation and view-resolution trade-offs, and supplies useful implementation, reconstruction, prompt, data-split, and user-study details in the supplement.
weaknesses: The evaluation scale is modest relative to the broad generalization claims: training uses only eight scenes, fully zero-shot scene evaluation covers four scenes and 14 scene-instruction cases, and the 100 reported cases are highly correlated by scene. No uncertainty estimates or repeated-run variance are reported.

The validation of VGGT confidence as a consistency verifier is suggestive but confounded. Progressively replacing original views with independently edited views changes semantics and image distribution as well as geometric consistency. Controlled perturbations, correlations with ground-truth geometric error, and comparison against human consistency judgments would establish the claim more convincingly.

The primary consistency metric uses depths inferred by VGGT, while VGGT also supplies the training rewards. This creates potential evaluator alignment and weakens the independence of the consistency evidence. A separate reconstruction model, correspondence metric, or geometry-based human evaluation would strengthen the case.

VIEScore is GPT-4.1-based and is characterized too strongly as objective and reproducible. The manuscript does not report evaluator prompts, sampling settings, repeated judgments, or score variance. Likewise, the 25-person user study lacks confidence intervals and sufficiently detailed assignment and randomization procedures.

Most ablations are trained and tested only on a face scene with roughly 200 samples. This is useful diagnostic evidence, but it does not establish that the same reward behavior and chosen weights hold for complex outdoor scenes, stylized edits, or large geometry changes.

The comparison set omits some closely related recent feed-forward multi-view editing work discussed in the paper, most notably Tinker. If code or models are unavailable, that limitation should be stated explicitly and qualitative or reported-number comparisons considered.

The wording “single-pass” and “optimization-free” is potentially misleading because producing the final editable 3D scene still involves AnySplat initialization followed by 3,000 iterations of scene-specific 3DGS optimization. The genuine advantage is avoiding per-scene optimization of the editing model, not eliminating reconstruction optimization.

Reproducibility is promising but incomplete: code and model release are only promised, and several consequential optimization details are not fully specified. Given the expensive 42-hour GRPO training process and stochastic rewards, released training code and seeds will be particularly important.
